meta.title: Homebase workout mode: verified evidence register
meta.purpose: The only list of science claims and training formulas the app may use. Anything not in 'kept' must not appear in the app. 'dropped' is recorded so nobody re-adds it by accident.
rules: Only 'kept' entries may be shown or used. Show 'correctedClaim' word for word; never the original research wording.
The badge always comes from 'correctGrade'. Never raise it.

An entry reaches an exercise page only through its 'showOn' list. 'this' = the claim is about this exercise. 'variation' = tested on a similar exercise, never this exact one; the page must say so. 'category' = about a whole group (all band exercises, all core exercises); the page must say so.
Sources with citeInApp:false are kept here for the record and are never shown in the app.
Sources with addedFromVerification:true were not in the original research list but were opened by the verifier and support wording in correctedClaim.

appUse 'not-in-v1' = verified but not built in the first release. 'info:*' = explained on an info sheet using the plain summary written in SPEC.md, with correctedClaim shown under 'Study details'. 'trainingMath.*' / 'rule:*' = drives a calculation.
Anything the app does that is not backed by a kept entry is an app convention: it is listed in SPEC.md and never gets a badge.
A build-time test must fail if any dropped id appears anywhere in src/, or if any id used in src/ is not in kept.
dropRules: Verdict 'wrong' is dropped. The verifier's replacement sentence was not independently re-checked, so it is not used.
A claim that rests on a retracted paper is dropped.
A claim the research itself says not to adopt is dropped.
A duplicate whose numbers conflict with a more carefully checked kept claim is dropped.

gradeScheme.A: Measured over weeks: people trained for weeks and the named outcome (usually muscle size by MRI or ultrasound, sometimes strength or fat) was measured before and after. One small study still counts; the claim text says how small. A means the right kind of evidence, not settled science.
gradeScheme.B: Measured in one session only: muscle activity sensors (EMG), leverage or load measurements, or rating studies. It shows what happens during a lift, not what grows.
gradeScheme.C: Reasoned, not tested: anatomy, physics, arithmetic, or an app convention. Plausible, but no study measured this exact claim.

kept.correctedClaim: Full-depth squats grew the glutes and inner-thigh adductors about two to three times more than half squats, while front-thigh growth was about the same.

sources.citation: Kubo K, Ikebukuro T, Yata H. Effects of squat training with different depths on lower limb muscle volumes. Eur J Appl Physiol. 2019;119(9):1933-1942. doi:10.1007/s00421-019-04181-y

kept.evidence: Opened the Europe PMC record (https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=EXT_ID:31230110%20AND%20SRC:MED&resultType=core&format=json, same paper as https://europepmc.org/article/MED/31230110) and a full-text PDF copy (https://highfit.com.br/wp-content/uploads/2019/06/KEITARO-KUBO-2019.pdf). Kubo, Ikebukuro, Yata, Eur J Appl Physiol 2019;119:1933-1942 exists as cited. MRI muscle volume, 10 weeks, 2 days/week. Knee extensors +4.9% (full) vs +4.6% (half). Adductors +6.2% vs +2.7% (p=0.026). Gluteus maximus +6.7% vs +2.2% (p=0.008). The numbers match. Scope: 17 untrained young men (8 vs 9). 'Full' meant about 140 degrees of knee bend and 'half' about 90 degrees. The half-squat group's glutes and adductors did still grow significantly.

kept.correctedClaim: In 17 young men over 12 weeks, deep squats (knee bent to about 120°) grew the front of the thigh at every measured spot (4–7%), while shallow squats (about 60°) grew it only near the hip, so deep squats came out ahead.

sources.citation: Bloomquist K, Langberg H, Karlsen S, et al. Effect of range of motion in heavy load squatting on muscle and tendon adaptations. Eur J Appl Physiol. 2013;113(8):2133-2142. doi:10.1007/s00421-013-2642-7
Kubo K, Ikebukuro T, Yata H. Eur J Appl Physiol. 2019;119(9):1933-1942. doi:10.1007/s00421-019-04181-y

kept.evidence: Opened the Europe PMC record for PMID 23604798 and a full-text PDF (https://highfit.com.br/wp-content/uploads/2017/03/Squat-BLOOMQUIST-2013.pdf). Bloomquist et al., Eur J Appl Physiol 2013;113:2133-2142, randomized, MRI cross-sectional area. Full text: front-thigh area 'was increased at all measured sites in the DS group (4–7%), while increases at the two most proximal sites were observed in the SS group', and the change was greater for DS at all sites. The gradeWhy misreads this: 4–7% is the deep group's own gain, not how much 'better' it was. The 'front thigh' measure included sartorius, plus the adductors in the top slices. Subjects were sports-science students who were not squatting more than once a week. Sessions were rep-matched, so the shallow group lifted much heavier loads. The idea that the benefit comes 'mainly from avoiding very shallow squats' is the writer's inference from comparing Kubo 2019's 90° vs 140° with this study's 60° vs 120° (grade C). No study tested it directly.

kept.correctedClaim: Myth check: in small 9–12 week MRI studies of young, mostly untrained adults, squats grew the hamstrings little or not at all. One found no change in whole-muscle volume, one found none at a single upper-thigh slice, and a third found a gain at only one of six spots.

sources.citation: Kubo K, Ikebukuro T, Yata H. Eur J Appl Physiol. 2019;119(9):1933-1942. doi:10.1007/s00421-019-04181-y

Plotkin DL, Rodas MA, Vigotsky AD, et al. Hip thrust and back squat training elicit similar gluteus muscle hypertrophy and transfer similarly to the deadlift. Front Physiol. 2023;14:1279170. doi:10.3389/fphys.2023.1279170
Bloomquist K, Langberg H, Karlsen S, et al. Eur J Appl Physiol. 2013;113(8):2133-2142. doi:10.1007/s00421-013-2642-7

kept.evidence: Kubo 2019 (Europe PMC record for PMID 31230110, plus the full-text PDF): hamstring volume 'did not change in either group' (whole-muscle MRI volume, 17 untrained men). Plotkin 2023 (full text via Europe PMC PMC10593473, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10593473/): hamstrings showed 'little to no growth' and there was 'no meaningful growth in either group'. But Plotkin measured the thigh at only ONE slice just below the glutes, with participants lying prone on the coil. The authors say compression may have affected the thigh and distal measures were not taken, so this is weaker than a whole-muscle test. A third MRI study the claim leaves out, Bloomquist 2013 (full-text PDF above), found that deep squats increased back-thigh area at the second-most-proximal of six sites. So calling it 'no measurable growth' in every MRI study is too strong, but 'little' holds.

kept.correctedClaim: In one 10-week MRI study, squats grew the quadriceps overall but not the rectus femoris, the one quad muscle that also crosses the hip; the leg press showed the same pattern in a separate study.

sources.citation: Kubo K, Ikebukuro T, Yata H. Eur J Appl Physiol. 2019;119(9):1933-1942. doi:10.1007/s00421-019-04181-y

Kinoshita M, Maeo S, Kobayashi Y, et al. Hypertrophic Effects of Single- versus Multi-Joint Exercise: A Direct Comparison between Knee Extension and Leg Press. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2026;58(7):1566-1580. doi:10.1249/mss.0000000000003957

kept.evidence: Kubo 2019 (Europe PMC record for PMID 31230110 and the full-text PDF): knee-extensor volume +4.9%/+4.6%, 'whereas that of rectus femoris and hamstring muscles did not change in either group' (MRI volume). Kinoshita 2026, Med Sci Sports Exerc 58(7):1566-1580, full text via Europe PMC PMC13215645: rectus femoris +1.1% after leg press, P=0.379, versus +13.2% after leg extension. The direct squat evidence is one study of 17 untrained men, and the leg-press data only support the pattern rather than testing squats. The claim as written is accurate, but the page should say it comes from one study.

kept.correctedClaim: Over 9 weeks, hip thrusts and back squats grew the glutes about equally in beginners, but squats also grew the quads and adductors more.

sources.citation: Plotkin DL, Rodas MA, Vigotsky AD, et al. Front Physiol. 2023;14:1279170. doi:10.3389/fphys.2023.1279170
Barbalho M, Coswig V, Souza D, et al. Back Squat vs. Hip Thrust Resistance-training Programs in Well-trained Women. Int J Sports Med. 2020;41(5):306-310. doi:10.1055/a-1082-1126
sources.why: Named among papers flagged in 2020 as having improbable data; same group has four retractions.

sources.citation: Barbalho M, Coswig VS, Steele J, et al. Evidence for an Upper Threshold for Resistance Training Volume in Trained Women. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2019;51(3):515-522 (RETRACTED 2021)

kept.evidence: Plotkin 2023 full text (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10593473/, pulled via Europe PMC). 34 untrained adults (18 hip thrust: 5 men, 13 women; 16 squat: 6 men, 10 women), set-equated, 9 weeks. MRI cross-sectional area at single slices, not whole-muscle volume. Glute estimates modestly favored hip thrusts: lower −1.6 cm² (CI −6.1 to 2.0), mid −0.5, upper −0.5, all with CIs crossing zero. Squats grew more quadriceps (3.6 cm², CI 0.7–6.4) and adductors (2.5 cm², CI 1.2–3.9). Barbalho 2020 (Europe PMC record for PMID 31975359): 22 well-trained women, 12 weeks. Ultrasound muscle THICKNESS (not MRI) favored squats for the glutes (9.4% vs 3.7%). It is not marked retracted. Correction to the gradeWhy: Retraction Watch (https://retractionwatch.com/2021/12/17/exercise-researcher-earns-more-retractions-as-investigations-mount/) lists this exact hip thrust paper among the seven that data sleuths asked to have retracted in June 2020 as having improbable data. So the doubt is about this paper itself, not only about its authors' other papers. Europe PMC does index four retracted Barbalho papers (MSSE 2019, IJSPP 2020, EJSS 2020, JSCR 2020), so 'four others retracted' holds. The MSSE 2019 retraction is confirmed (Retraction in MSSE 2021;53(6):1318).

kept.correctedClaim: Myth check: hip thrusts switched on the glutes more than squats, but in the same study of beginners that extra activation did not reliably turn into extra glute growth.

sources.citation: Plotkin DL, Rodas MA, Vigotsky AD, et al. Front Physiol. 2023;14:1279170. doi:10.3389/fphys.2023.1279170

Vigotsky AD, Halperin I, Lehman GJ, Trajano GS, Vieira TM. Interpreting Signal Amplitudes in Surface Electromyography Studies in Sport and Rehabilitation Sciences. Front Physiol. 2017;8:985. doi:10.3389/fphys.2017.00985

kept.evidence: Plotkin 2023 full text (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10593473/). Average glute EMG was higher for hip thrusts at all sites (p<0.01), but peak EMG was higher only at the upper and middle glute max. EMG was recorded during one 10RM set in the first session. Growth was similar between groups. The authors say sEMG differences 'did not reliably translate to greater hypertrophy, no matter what analytical approach we took'. One nuance: the upper glute site showed a moderate across-person correlation (r=0.50, CI 0.03–0.81), and its indirect-effect CI excluded zero. So 'not consistently' is exact and 'never' would be wrong. The claim avoids saying 'never'. Vigotsky 2017, Front Physiol 8:985 exists (Europe PMC record for PMID 29354060). It is a general review on limits of EMG interpretation, background only. Calling Plotkin 'the clearest direct test' is editorial and should not be shown as a finding. One study, 34 untrained adults.

kept.correctedClaim: With estimated 10-rep-max weights, the barbell hip thrust produced roughly twice the average glute activity of the back squat, with similar front-thigh activity, in 13 trained women.

sources.citation: Contreras B, Vigotsky AD, Schoenfeld BJ, Beardsley C, Cronin J. A Comparison of Gluteus Maximus, Biceps Femoris, and Vastus Lateralis Electromyographic Activity in the Back Squat and Barbell Hip Thrust Exercises. J Appl Biomech. 2015;31(6):452-458. doi:10.1123/jab.2014-0301

kept.evidence: Europe PMC record for PMID 26214739 (https://europepmc.org/article/MED/26214739). Contreras et al., J Appl Biomech 2015;31(6):452-458. Thirteen trained women, estimated 10RM loads. Mean upper glute max 69.5% vs 29.4%, lower glute max 86.8% vs 45.4% (2.4x and 1.9x). Vastus lateralis mean 99.5% vs 110%, not significant. The abstract ends saying longitudinal training studies are needed. EMG only, so B is correct.

kept.correctedClaim: Neither hip thrusts nor squats grew the side glutes (glute medius and minimus) much in beginners over 9 weeks.

sources.citation: Plotkin DL, Rodas MA, Vigotsky AD, et al. Front Physiol. 2023;14:1279170. doi:10.3389/fphys.2023.1279170

kept.evidence: Plotkin 2023 full text (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10593473/). Abstract: gluteus medius + minimus 'demonstrated little to no growth'. Discussion: 'meaningful growth occurring, except in the gluteus medius and minimus'. The two muscles were measured together at one MRI slice (the upper glute max level), not as whole-muscle volume. Separate support: Kinoshita 2026 (full text, PMC13215645) Table 1 shows no significant glute medius or minimus change after 12 weeks of leg press or leg extension (whole-muscle MRI volume). One study for these two exercises, untrained adults. It does not show which exercise would grow these muscles.

kept.correctedClaim: The glute bridge uses the same hip-straightening action as the hip thrust over a shorter range, so the glutes are expected to do most of the work with the hamstrings helping.
kept.evidence: No source was cited, and none exists to open for this sentence. It is joint-action reasoning, which is correctly graded C. I made one wording change: 'do most of the work' becomes 'are expected to', because no EMG or growth data for the floor bridge were checked.

kept.correctedClaim: In 17 untrained adults training one leg on each machine for 12 weeks, the leg press grew the gluteus maximus about 15% and the adductor magnus about 6%, but not the glute medius or minimus, and it grew the three vasti (front-thigh muscles) as much as leg extensions did.

sources.citation: Kinoshita M, Maeo S, Kobayashi Y, et al. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2026;58(7):1566-1580. doi:10.1249/mss.0000000000003957

kept.evidence: Full text via Europe PMC PMC13215645 (https://europepmc.org/article/MED/41630124). Kinoshita et al., Med Sci Sports Exerc 2026;58(7):1566-1580. MRI volume of 17 muscles, 11 men and 6 women, untrained, one leg per exercise. Leg-press knee range 90°→0°, hip 90°→60°. Gluteus maximus +15.4% and adductor magnus +6.2% after leg press, but not after leg extension (−0.9% to +0.2%). Vasti: VL 6.4 vs 6.2%, VM 7.2 vs 6.0%, VI 5.0 vs 4.4%, no interaction. The original sentence says 'the glutes', which overstates it. In Table 1, gluteus medius (290.8→305.1 cm³, not significant) and gluteus minimus (83.1→85.0) did not significantly grow. Only the gluteus maximus did.

kept.correctedClaim: In a 12-week MRI study of untrained adults, leg extensions grew the rectus femoris about 13% while leg presses grew it about 1% (not a real change); a smaller ultrasound study whose measurement method was disputed points the same way.

sources.citation: Kinoshita M, Maeo S, Kobayashi Y, et al. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2026;58(7):1566-1580. doi:10.1249/mss.0000000000003957

Zabaleta-Korta A, Fernández-Peña E, Torres-Unda J, Garbisu-Hualde A, Santos-Concejero J. The role of exercise selection in regional muscle hypertrophy: A randomized controlled trial. J Sports Sci. 2021;39(20):2298-2304. doi:10.1080/02640414.2021.1929736
Leitão BFM, Franchi MV, da Matta TT. Letter to the editor concerning the article by Zabaleta-Korta et al. (2021). J Sports Sci. 2022;40(6):655-657. doi:10.1080/02640414.2021.2013596

kept.evidence: Kinoshita 2026 full text (PMC13215645): rectus femoris +13.2% (KE, P<0.001) vs +1.1% (LP, P=0.379), 17 untrained adults, MRI volume. Zabaleta-Korta 2021 (Europe PMC record for PMID 34743671): abstract says all three RF regions grew in the leg-extension group, and only central VL grew in the Smith-squat group. I could not open the full text, so its sample size and training status are unverified. The Leitão, Franchi, da Matta 2022 letter was opened via its Semantic Scholar record (https://api.semanticscholar.org/graph/v1/paper/DOI:10.1080/02640414.2021.2013596). It argues the study's ultrasound 'CSA' measures 'are not representative of true muscle CSA'. In their reply (DOI 10.1080/02640414.2022.2052596), the authors agree MRI is the gold standard. So the second study is weaker than presented. 'The dependable way' implies more replication and generality than one MRI study in untrained people plus one disputed ultrasound study.

kept.correctedClaim: Leg extensions done only in the bottom half, where the knee is bent and the quads are stretched, grew parts of the thigh more than full-range or top-half reps in untrained women.

sources.citation: Pedrosa GF, Lima FV, Schoenfeld BJ, et al. Partial range of motion training elicits favorable improvements in muscular adaptations when carried out at long muscle lengths. Eur J Sport Sci. 2022;22(8):1250-1260. doi:10.1080/17461391.2021.1927199

Plotkin DL, Tiede DR, Gotla T, et al. Acute molecular and chronic vastus lateralis adaptations to lengthened partial versus full range of motion resistance training in previously trained males. Preprint, 2026. doi:10.64898/2026.06.04.730150
sources.why: Preprint, not peer reviewed; kept only as background in the evidence record.

sources.citation: Varovic D, Wolf M, Schoenfeld BJ, Steele J, Grgic J, Mikulic P. Does Muscle Length Influence Regional Hypertrophy? A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. Int J Sports Med. 2025;46(14):1027-1036. doi:10.1055/a-2615-4935

kept.evidence: Europe PMC record for PMID 33977835. Pedrosa et al., Eur J Sport Sci 2022;22(8):1250-1260, randomized, 45 untrained women. Initial partial range (100–65°) had a greater relative increase than ALL groups at 70% of femur length. At 50% and 60% it beat full-range, top-half and control, but NOT the varied-range group. RF and VL cross-sectional area was measured at 40–70% of femur length. The measurement method was not confirmed from the full text. The 2026 preprint exists (bioRxiv API record https://api.biorxiv.org/details/biorxiv/10.64898/2026.06.04.730150, posted 2026-06-09, not peer reviewed). It had 16 trained men with one leg per condition for 8 weeks, and found no clear VL difference (LP−FULL −1.4 cm², CI −6.1 to 3.8). But the lengthened partials were applied across THREE exercises (leg press, leg extension, lying leg curl), not leg extension alone. The uncited '2025 meta-analysis' is real: Varović et al., Int J Sports Med 2025, doi:10.1055/a-2615-4935 (opened via Semantic Scholar and SportRxiv https://sportrxiv.org/index.php/server/preprint/view/464). It found trivial differences between longer and shorter muscle-length training at proximal, mid and distal sites (SMD 0.05, 0.07, 0.09). Add it as a source.

kept.correctedClaim: Seated leg curls grew the hamstrings more than lying leg curls (about 14% vs 9%), likely because the bent hip keeps the hamstrings stretched.

sources.citation: Maeo S, Huang M, Wu Y, et al. Greater Hamstrings Muscle Hypertrophy but Similar Damage Protection after Training at Long versus Short Muscle Lengths. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2021;53(4):825-837. doi:10.1249/MSS.0000000000002523

kept.evidence: Full text via Europe PMC PMC7969179 (https://europepmc.org/article/MED/33009197). Maeo et al., Med Sci Sports Exerc 2021;53(4):825-837. 20 young adults with no systematic resistance training in the past 12 months, one leg per exercise, 12 weeks, MRI volume. Whole hamstrings +14% vs +9%. The two-joint muscles +8–24% vs +4–19%. The one-joint short head +10% vs +9%. An OpenSim model in the paper shows the two-joint hamstrings work at longer lengths when seated, and there is no difference for the short head. That supports the stretch explanation, labeled 'likely'. Untrained, one study.

kept.correctedClaim: A straight-knee 45° hip-extension exercise grew the outer hamstring (biceps femoris long head) more than Nordic curls, while both grew the inner semitendinosus.

sources.citation: Bourne MN, Duhig SJ, Timmins RG, et al. Impact of the Nordic hamstring and hip extension exercises on hamstring architecture and morphology: implications for injury prevention. Br J Sports Med. 2017;51(5):469-477. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2016-096130

kept.evidence: Europe PMC record for PMID 27660368 (https://europepmc.org/article/MED/27660368). Bourne et al., Br J Sports Med 2017;51(5):469-477, randomized, 30 recreationally active men (10 per group), 10 weeks. MRI: BFlh volume increased more with hip extension than Nordic (d=1.03, p=0.037). Semitendinosus rose in both vs control (d=2.16–2.50), not different between exercises (p=0.239). The record lists a 2019 correction (Br J Sports Med 53(6):e2) whose content I could not open. Separate support from Maeo et al. 2024, MSSE, doi:10.1249/mss.0000000000003490 (Europe PMC record for PMID 38857522): in 42 men, hip-flexed eccentric curls grew BFlh +19% vs +5% for Nordics (MRI).

kept.correctedClaim: Nordic curls grew the semitendinosus and lengthened the fascicles (fibre bundles) of the outer hamstring. Hip extensions and Romanian deadlifts lengthened them just as much, and the lengthening faded within two weeks of stopping.

sources.citation: Bourne MN, Duhig SJ, Timmins RG, et al. Br J Sports Med. 2017;51(5):469-477. doi:10.1136/bjsports-2016-096130

Arin-Bal G, Comlekci M, Pakoz B, Uysal O, Bayrakci-Tunay V. Effect of Hamstring Exercises on Morphological Parameters of the Hamstring Muscle: A Systematic Review With MRI and USI Findings. Sports Health. 2026. doi:10.1177/19417381261463404
Crawford et al. Med Sci Sports Exerc. 2025. doi:10.1249/mss.0000000000003701

kept.evidence: Bourne 2017 (Europe PMC record for PMID 27660368): Nordic training increased semitendinosus volume vs control (MRI) and lengthened BFlh fascicles (2D ultrasound, d=1.77–2.17). But hip extension lengthened them equally (between-exercise p=0.279–0.976). Arin-Bal 2026 review (Europe PMC record for PMID 42460513, full text PMC13375868): 14 trials. Eccentric protocols, 'particularly NHE-based', were 'most consistently' linked to longer BFlh fascicles, while size changes were 'more heterogeneous'. It is a systematic review without a meta-analysis. Crawford et al. 2025, MSSE, doi:10.1249/mss.0000000000003701 (Europe PMC record for PMID 40085810): 32 young adults, 6 weeks. Eccentric-emphasis Romanian deadlifts and Nordics gave the same fascicle lengthening (~9%) and hamstring area gain (~10%). Fascicle length 'returned to baseline after detraining' (2 weeks). Maeo 2024 (PMID 38857522): Nordics grew the whole hamstrings +11% but BFlh only +5%. So fascicle lengthening is real, but it is not special to Nordics. The sentence implies it is.

kept.correctedClaim: The Romanian deadlift bends at the hips with nearly straight knees, so it loads the hamstrings and glutes while they are stretched.

sources.citation: Bourne MN, Duhig SJ, Timmins RG, et al. Br J Sports Med. 2017;51(5):469-477 (related exercise, not the RDL). doi:10.1136/bjsports-2016-096130

kept.evidence: The sentence itself is anatomy reasoning, correctly graded C. The gradeWhy is out of date: 'the Romanian deadlift itself has not been growth-tested' is refuted. Crawford et al., Med Sci Sports Exerc 2025, doi:10.1249/mss.0000000000003701 (Europe PMC record for PMID 40085810, found via the reference list of the Arin-Bal 2026 review, PMC13375868). It randomized 32 young adults to eccentric-emphasis RDLs or Nordics for 6 weeks. Hamstring cross-sectional area (ultrasound) rose about 10% with no difference between groups. Longer BFlh fascicles also showed no group difference. That supports a separate measured-growth line for the RDL (A, one small ultrasound study), which the app could add instead of pointing to Bourne 2017's related exercise.

kept.correctedClaim: The conventional deadlift straightens the hips and knees at the same time, so the hip extensors (glutes, adductors, hamstrings) and back muscles carry the load, the quads help mostly as the bar leaves the floor, and the hamstrings change length less than in a Romanian deadlift.
kept.evidence: No source was cited and none was opened, so this stays pure joint-action reasoning (C). 'The quads do most of the work' and the implication that the hamstrings contribute little are claims about how the work is split. No EMG or modeling source here supports that. The part that holds is the length logic: hip and knee straighten together, so the two-joint hamstrings change length less. The rewrite keeps only what the reasoning supports.

kept.correctedClaim: Standing calf raises grew the gastrocnemius by about 9–12%, while seated calf raises barely grew it (under 2%).

sources.citation: Kinoshita M, Maeo S, Kobayashi Y, et al. Triceps surae muscle hypertrophy is greater after standing versus seated calf-raise training. Front Physiol. 2023;14:1272106. doi:10.3389/fphys.2023.1272106

kept.evidence: Full text via Europe PMC PMC10753835 (https://europepmc.org/article/MED/38156065). Kinoshita et al., Front Physiol 2023;14:1272106 (a brief report). 14 untrained adults, one leg standing and one seated (knee 90°), 70% 1RM, 12 weeks, MRI volume. Lateral gastrocnemius 12.4% vs 1.7%, medial 9.2% vs 0.6%. The seated-leg gastrocnemius changes were not significant (p=0.147–0.508). The soleus was similar (2.1% vs 2.9%). The numbers match. Small sample, untrained people.

kept.correctedClaim: Myth check: in one 12-week MRI study of 14 untrained adults, seated calf raises did not grow the soleus any more than standing calf raises did (2.9% vs 2.1%, not a significant difference), so 'seated for the soleus' is unproven.

sources.citation: Kinoshita M, Maeo S, Kobayashi Y, et al. Front Physiol. 2023;14:1272106. doi:10.3389/fphys.2023.1272106

kept.evidence: Opened the Europe PMC record (https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/search?query=EXT_ID:38156065%20AND%20SRC:MED&resultType=core&format=json; same as https://europepmc.org/article/MED/38156065). Kinoshita et al., Front Physiol 2023, title 'Triceps surae muscle hypertrophy is greater after standing versus seated calf-raise training'. Fourteen UNTRAINED adults, one leg standing/knee-extended, other leg seated/knee 90°, 70% 1RM, 5x10, 2x/week, 12 weeks, MRI muscle volume. Soleus change 'similar between legs (2.1% vs. 2.1%... )' exactly: standing 2.1% vs seated 2.9%, p = 0.410. Numbers and design match. Caveat to keep: untrained people, within-person design, small sample so a small true difference could be missed.

kept.correctedClaim: In one 8-week ultrasound study of 42 young women doing calf raises on a leg-press machine, bottom-half (stretched) reps grew the inner calf head more than full-range or top-half reps, but for the outer calf head they only beat top-half reps, not full-range reps.

Medial and posterior delts were more active in behind-the-neck presses, and pectoralis major in front presses. I also opened Saeterbakken and Fimland 2013 (JSCR, PMID 23096062, 15 men), which measured anterior, medial and posterior delts, biceps and triceps across press variations. Neither study ranks the side delt as a minor helper. I could not pull absolute EMG levels from the figures, so the 'mainly front delts, side delts assisting' ranking is unconfirmed. Joint-action reasoning (shoulder flexion plus abduction) makes the side delt a major contributor, not an assistant, and the claim leaves out the upper chest.

kept.correctedClaim: Myth check: cable and dumbbell lateral raises grew the side delts by similar amounts in trained lifters, even though cables keep more tension at the bottom.

kept.evidence: Opened PMC12277279 (Larsen et al., Front Physiol 2025, doi:10.3389/fphys.2025.1611468). 26 randomized, 24 completed (16 men, 8 women), resistance-trained (about 7.1 years), one arm per method, 8 weeks, 16 sessions, B-mode ultrasound at 2 sites. Cable +3.3–4.6%, dumbbell +3.4–3.9%. Bayes factors were 0.22 and 0.27 (moderate support for no difference), and the multivariate BF was below 0.01. The authors list as limitations the short duration and ultrasound error (about 0.4 mm) that is large next to the 0.5–1 mm changes. 'Similar' is slightly more exact than 'equally', but the grade note already covers this.

kept.correctedClaim: Overhead cable triceps extensions grew the whole triceps about 1.4 times more than pushdowns (about 20% vs 14%), even though lighter weights were used.

kept.correctedClaim: Myth check: overhead extensions did not just grow the long head, because the lateral and medial heads that pushdowns supposedly target also grew more with overhead work.
kept.evidence: Same Maeo 2023 abstract (PMID 35819335): the one-joint lateral plus medial heads grew 1.4-fold more with overhead work (+14.6% vs +10.5%, d=0.39, P=0.002). The abstract says only the two-joint long head is lengthened more overhead, so the one-joint heads' extra growth is not explained by stretch. One study.

kept.correctedClaim: Lying triceps extensions put the upper arm partway overhead, which stretches the triceps long head more than a pushdown but less than a full overhead extension.

kept.evidence: The Maeo 2023 abstract (PMID 35819335) confirms the mechanism: 'The biarticular triceps brachii long head (TBLong) is lengthened more in the overhead than neutral arm position.' The long head crosses the shoulder, so its length rises with shoulder flexion: about 0° in a pushdown, about 90° or more in a lying extension, near full flexion overhead. The in-between placement follows from anatomy, but no study of the skull crusher itself was found or opened, so C is correct and it should not be presented as tested.

kept.evidence: Varovic 2025, Int J Sports Med 46(14):1027-36 (Europe PMC REST, PMID 40570881): Bayesian meta-analysis of 12 studies in young adults. Trivial effects of longer vs shorter muscle-length training at the proximal (SMD 0.05), mid (0.07) and distal (0.09) sites, with 'an increasing trend from proximal to distal' and a high share within practical equivalence. The authors caution that the conditions differed by only about 21.8% mean muscle length. The wording is a small clarification: the analysis compared growth at each site, not a change in which part grows.

kept.correctedClaim: Mayhew 2008 reviewed 14 published 1RM equations and said most of them give no evidence of who they were built from or how they were fitted; it does not say this about Epley or Brzycki by name, and it credits the w*(1+0.0333*r) form to Welday 1988, not Epley. Treat both as working conventions whose origin I have not checked.

Methods: 'Most of the prediction equations gave no evidence of the population used to develop the equations or how they were derived statistically.' Table 2 lists Brzycki (7) = RepWt/(1.0278-0.0278 RTF) and 'Welday (35)' = (RTF x 0.0333) RepWt + RepWt; Epley is not cited anywhere. The sentence does not single out which equations lack a sample, so applying it to Epley and Brzycki specifically is an inference. Epley 1985 and Brzycki 1993 originals not opened.

kept.correctedClaim: 1RM estimates are more accurate from lower rep counts. In 70 adults (34 men, 36 women, aged 18-69), the fit was R^2 = 0.974 (leg press) and 0.993 (chest press) from a 5RM, dropping at 10RM and 20RM, and the authors advise no more than 10 reps. In 103 mostly untrained college women benching, Mayhew 2008 found predictions were more accurate below 10 reps to fatigue. A 2025 study in about 40 recreationally active men, tested only at 80% 1RM, recommended its two chosen equations for loads giving 4-10 reps to failure; it did not compare rep ranges.

The 4-10 range is a condition on their recommended equations, not a tested comparison.

kept.topic: Reps at %1RM vary by exercise and person
kept.correctedClaim: Nuzzo's meta-regression (269 studies, 7,289 people, 952 tests) found more reps in the leg press than the bench press at every load. At 70% 1RM the general model gives about 15 reps against 11 in the textbook table; bench about 14, leg press about 19. The spread between people is about 2.51 reps at 80% and 4.36 at 60%, so it grows as the load gets lighter.

Sports Med 2024;54(2):303-321 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10933212/, full text opened): '952 repetitions-to-failure tests, completed by 7289 individuals in 452 groups from 269 studies'; 'greater mean repetitions completed in the leg press than bench press across the spectrum of relative loads'; LP 70% = 19.0 [14.2-25.5], BP 70% = 14.1 [12.4-16.1]; 'in Table 1, estimates at 90% and 70% 1RM are 4 and 11 ... In Fig. 2 ... ~5 and ~15'; 'at 80% 1RM ... SD ... is 2.51 repetitions, whereas at 60% 1RM ... 4.36'. Groups were 66% male, 60% resistance trained.

kept.topic: Generic equations overestimate high-rep and leg-press sets
kept.correctedClaim: Putting Nuzzo's average reps into the equations: bench at 80% with about 9 reps gives Epley 1.04x and Brzycki 1.03x the true 1RM; leg press at 70% with about 19 reps gives 1.14x and 1.40x. So a generic equation with no rep cap or exercise correction will inflate leg-press and high-rep estimates for the average person. The multipliers are approximate, and the leg-press rep estimate itself has a wide range (14-26 reps at 70%).

kept.evidence: Arithmetic checked in a scratch script: 0.8*(1+9/30)=1.040, 0.8*36/28=1.029 (with the exact 8.8 reps: 1.035 and 1.021); 0.7*(1+19/30)=1.143, 0.7*36/18=1.400. Inputs from Nuzzo 2024 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10933212/): BP 80% = 8.8 reps, LP 70% = 19.0 reps [95% CI 14.2-25.5]. The CI means the leg-press multiplier could be anywhere from about 1.03 to 1.30 for Epley.

kept.correctedClaim: On the RIR-based RPE scale, RPE 10 = 0 reps in reserve, 9 = 1, 8 = 2, 7 = 3, 5-6 = 4-6, and RIR ratings are recommended mainly for sets at RPE 7-10. In one study experienced squatters rated true 1RMs closer to 10 than novices (9.80 vs 8.96), and ratings tracked bar speed more closely in experienced lifters (r = -0.88 vs -0.77). In 15 powerlifters, RPE at 1RM was 9.6-9.7 and %1RM correlated with RPE at r = 0.88-0.91.

kept.correctedClaim: On average people think they have fewer reps left than they really do, by about 0.95 reps (95% CI 0.17-1.73), but results vary hugely between studies. Accuracy was clearly worse in sets longer than 12 reps. Being closer to failure and being in a later set helped only slightly (the closer-to-failure effect was not clearly different from zero). Training status made no difference.

Sorting sets into direct and indirect was 'not wholly objective'. In their table, rows and pulldowns were indirect for biceps; bench and overhead presses were indirect for triceps; bench and chest press were indirect for front delts (shoulder press was direct); squats and leg press were indirect for rectus femoris; pulldowns and rows were the only (indirect) sets for traps; hamstrings had only leg curls (direct) and nothing indirect.

kept.correctedClaim: More weekly sets gave more muscle growth, with diminishing returns and no clear plateau. A square-root curve fit best; the slope was 0.24% per set (CrI 0.15-0.33) at about 12 sets. Efficiency bands (preprint): 4 minimum; 5-10 higher; 11-18 intermediate; 19-29 lower; 30-42 lowest; 43+ unclear. Few studies went past about 25 sets, and at high volumes the data also fit a plateau. Schoenfeld 2017 found 0.37% per extra set, and ACSM 2026 says growth is better with at least 10 sets a week.

kept.correctedClaim: Expert coaches agreed that a deload is a period of reduced training stress to shed physical and mental fatigue. kept.topic: Weekly fractional hard sets per muscle
kept.formulaAsResearched: Weekly fractional hard sets per muscle: S_m = SUM over sets s in window [ hard(s) * role(exercise(s), m) ];  role = 1.0 if m is a primary mover (direct), 0.5 if a meaningful synergist (indirect), 0 otherwise;  hard(s) = (s.kind == 'working') AND s.completed AND (s.rir is null OR s.rir <= T) (defaults: T = 3 (RPE >= 7), user-adjustable 0..5. Window = rolling 7 days including today, matching thisWeekCount. Sets with RIR unknown are counted but flagged 'effort not logged'. The 1 / 0.5 / 0 weights follow Pelland et al.; valid: Any number of sets. Show hypertrophy tiers (fractional sets/week, Pelland Table 2A): <4 below detectable minimum; 4 minimum effective dose; 5-10 higher efficiency; 11-18 intermediate; 19-29 lower; 30-42 lowest; 43+ unclear (little data above ~25).)
kept.correctedClaim: Weekly fractional hard sets per muscle: S_m = sum over sets of hard(s)*role(exercise, m); role = 1 for the main mover, 0.5 for a meaningful helper muscle, 0 otherwise (Pelland's 1/0.5/0 weights). hard(s) = working, completed, and RIR unknown or <= T (T = 3 by default; an app convention). Window = rolling 7 days. Show Pelland's growth bands as context: <4 below detectable; 4 minimum; 5-10 higher efficiency; 11-18 intermediate; 19-29 lower; 30-42 lowest; 43+ unclear. Caveats: Pelland counted all sets regardless of effort, and which exercises count as direct or indirect for each muscle is a judgement call.

kept.formulaAsResearched: Weekly fractional frequency per muscle: F_m = SUM over sessions d in window [ max over sets s in d of ( hard(s) * role(exercise(s), m) ) ] (defaults: A session with any direct set counts 1; a session with only indirect sets counts 0.5. Pelland's example: curls one day plus rows another gives total 2, fractional 1.5, direct 1.; valid: 0..7 for a 7-day window. Flag F_m < 2 for major muscles (ACSM 2026: at least 2 sessions/week).)
kept.correctedClaim: Weekly fractional frequency per muscle: F_m = sum over sessions of the largest hard(s)*role in that session. A session with any direct set counts 1; a session with only indirect sets counts 0.5 (Pelland's example: curls one day plus rows another gives total 2, fractional 1.5, direct 1). Flagging F_m < 2 for major muscles follows ACSM 2026's public advice to train all major muscle groups at least twice a week; the position stand ties 2+ sessions a week to strength, and with volume equal, frequency does not clearly change muscle growth.

sources.citation: Pelland JC et al. SportRxiv preprint 2024, section 2.4.
ACSM 2026 resistance training guidelines update page.

kept.evidence: Pelland preprint (https://sportrxiv.org/index.php/server/preprint/download/460/967) 2.4: '5 sets of biceps curls in one session and 5 sets of rows in another ... frequency quantified as total, fractional, and direct of 2, 1.5, and 1'. ACSM page (https://acsm.org/resistance-training-guidelines-update-2026/): 'Training all major muscle groups at least twice a week matters far more than chasing the idea of a perfect ... plan'. Currier 2026 abstract (PMID 41843416): '>=2 sessions/wk' listed under voluntary strength. Schoenfeld 2019 (PMID 30558493): no volume-equated frequency effect on growth. The < 2 cutoff applied to fractional frequency is an app convention, so C.

kept.topic: Strength volume band for one lift
kept.formulaAsResearched: Strength volume tier for a specific lift: S_lift = SUM over hard sets [ 1.0 if exercise == tested lift, 0.5 if exercise trains the lift's muscles, else 0 ] (defaults: Tiers (Pelland Table 2B, fractional sets/week): 1 minimum effective dose; 2 higher efficiency; 3-4 intermediate; 5+ gains no longer consistently exceed the smallest detectable effect (3.96%).; valid: Group-average model; lifters were mostly doing a new strength test. Show the tier for context only, never as a goal.)
kept.correctedClaim: Strength volume band for one lift: S_lift = sum over hard sets of 1.0 if it is the tested lift, 0.5 if it trains that lift's muscles, else 0. Pelland's strength bands (fractional sets per week): 1 minimum; 2 higher efficiency; 3-4 intermediate; 5+ extra sets no longer reliably add another detectable gain (3.96%). This is a group-average model in lifters who were mostly new to the strength test; show it for context, never as a goal.

sources.citation: Pelland JC et al. SportRxiv preprint 2024, Table 2B and section 5.5.

kept.evidence: Pelland preprint (https://sportrxiv.org/index.php/server/preprint/download/460/967) 2.4: strength direct = 'the exact exercise used for the strength assessment', indirect = 'likely to meaningfully train the muscle(s) involved'; Table 2B: Minimum Effective Dose 1; Higher Efficiency 2; Intermediate 3-4; Lower 5-? 'Additional weekly sets do not consistently enhance strength gains > SDES'; 5.5 novel-test learning effect.

kept.formulaAsResearched: Volume load (tonnage), per exercise: VL_exercise = SUM over working sets (w * r)   [same unit only; exclude sets where w <= 0] (defaults: Warm-ups excluded. Bodyweight and band sets are left out and reported as a rep count instead, which fixes the current unit mixing in workoutVolume().; valid: Only compare within the same exercise and rep range over time. Never add up across exercises as a growth or hypertrophy score.)
kept.correctedClaim: Volume load (tonnage) per exercise: sum over working sets of w*r, same unit only, excluding sets with w <= 0; warm-ups excluded; bodyweight and band sets reported as rep counts. Compare only within the same exercise and rep range over time, and never add it up across exercises as a growth score, because light and heavy loads to failure gave similar growth despite very different reps (Schoenfeld 2015). App convention built on that inference.

sources.citation: Schoenfeld BJ et al. Effects of low- vs high-load resistance training on muscle strength and hypertrophy in well-trained men. J Strength Cond Res 2015;29(10):2954-2963.

kept.evidence: Schoenfeld 2015, PMID 25853914 (Europe PMC abstract): 25-35 vs 8-12 reps to failure gave similar quad growth (9.5% vs 9.3%). The abstract does not report tonnage, so the rule rests on inference (see W3). The formula is a bookkeeping convention, so C.

kept.formulaAsResearched: Double progression (load step rule): if min(r over working sets) >= hi AND all RIR >= RIR_floor: w_next = ceilToLoadable( w * (1 + p) ), with w_next >= w + minIncrement;  elif r < lo on any working set in 2 consecutive sessions: w_next = floorToLoadable( w * 0.95 );  else: w_next = w (aim for +1 rep) (defaults: Rep range [lo, hi] from the routine (e.g. 6-8). RIR_floor = 1. p = 0.025. minIncrement = 5 lb / 2.5 kg for barbell lifts, or the next dumbbell or pin step. ACSM 2009 variant: trigger at r >= hi + 1 with p in 0.02..0.10.; valid: p in 0.02..0.10. lo < hi. Not for bodyweight or band work; for those, progress reps or band level instead.)
kept.correctedClaim: Double progression load step: if every working set reaches the top of the rep range with RIR >= 1, raise load by about 2.5% rounded up to a loadable step (at least 5 lb / 2.5 kg for barbells); if any working set falls below the bottom of the range in 2 sessions in a row, drop about 5%; otherwise keep the load and aim for +1 rep. ACSM 2009 variant: add 2-10% once the lifter beats the target by 1-2 reps. All specific numbers here (2.5%, RIR 1, 5% drop, 2 sessions) are app conventions; not for bodyweight or band work.

sources.citation: ACSM Position Stand. Progression models in resistance training for healthy adults. Med Sci Sports Exerc 2009;41(3):687-708 (abstract).

kept.evidence: ACSM 2009, MSSE 41(3):687-708 (Europe PMC abstract, URL as cited): '2-10% increase in load be applied when the individual can perform the current workload for one to two repetitions over the desired number'. Expert recommendation, never tested against alternatives; the app's thresholds are not in any source, so C, not B.

kept.formulaAsResearched: RPE autoregulation load adjustment: if RPE > RPE_hi: adj = -0.02 * (RPE - RPE_hi)/0.5;  if RPE < RPE_lo: adj = +0.02 * (RPE_lo - RPE)/0.5;  else adj = 0;  w_next_set = roundToLoadable( w * (1 + adj) ) (defaults: 2% load change per 0.5 RPE outside the target band. This was the protocol used in Helms 2018; it was not tested against other step sizes.; valid: RPE 6..10. Cap |adj| at 0.10 per set.)
kept.correctedClaim: RPE autoregulation: for each 0.5 RPE above the target band lower the next set's load 2%; for each 0.5 below, raise it 2%; round to a loadable weight. This is the protocol from Helms 2018 (21 trained men, 8 weeks), where RPE loading worked about as well as %1RM loading; the 2% step was not tested against other steps, and the 10% per-set cap is an app convention.

sources.citation: Helms ER et al. RPE vs. percentage 1RM loading in periodized programs matched for sets and repetitions. Front Physiol 2018;9:247.

kept.evidence: Helms 2018 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5877330/): 'For every 0.5 RPE above or below the upper or lower RPE threshold, respectively, load was decreased or increased by 2%'; both groups improved, no significant between-group differences.

kept.formulaAsResearched: Rest timer default: rest_s = 120 if exercise.isCompound else 90;  warn if logged rest_s < 60 on a hypertrophy-goal exercise (defaults: 120 s compound, 90 s isolation, user-editable. Option of 180 s for heavy (<= 5 reps) strength sets.; valid: 30..300 s. There is evidence of a small hypertrophy cost at <= 60 s and little evidence of extra benefit beyond 90 s.)
kept.correctedClaim: Default rest timer: 120 s for compound lifts, 90 s for isolation, editable, with an option of 180 s for heavy sets of 5 or fewer reps; warn if rest under 60 s on a growth-goal exercise. These defaults are app conventions. The evidence suggests a small, uncertain growth benefit from resting over 60 s, no clear extra benefit beyond 90 s, and one trial in trained men found 3 min beat 1 min for strength and thigh growth.

sources.citation: Singer A et al. Give it a rest: systematic review with Bayesian meta-analysis on inter-set rest interval duration and hypertrophy. Front Sports Act Living 2024;6:1429789.
Schoenfeld BJ et al. Longer interset rest periods enhance muscle strength and hypertrophy in resistance-trained men. J Strength Cond Res 2016;30(7):1805-1812.

kept.evidence: Singer 2024 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11349676/): '>60 s' benefit arm 0.13 (CrI -0.27 to 0.51), thigh 0.17 (-0.13 to 0.43); 'did not detect appreciable differences in hypertrophy when resting >90 s'. Schoenfeld 2016 (PMID 26605807): 3 min > 1 min in 21 trained men. 'Evidence of a small hypertrophy cost at <= 60 s' overstates CrIs that include zero. The 120/90 split is not from any source.
kept.appUse: trainingMath.defaultRest (the under-60-s warning is NOT built in v1)

kept.formulaAsResearched: Plate loading (per side + loadable rounding): fixed = bar + 2*collar;  step = 2 * minPlate;  loadable(target) = fixed + step * round((target - fixed)/step);  perSide = (loadable - fixed)/2;  plates = minCountDP(perSide, inventoryPairs) listed heaviest first (innermost) (defaults: lb: bar 45, collar 0, plates [45,35,25,10,5,2.5], step 5. kg: bar 20, collar 0 in a gym (2.5 each in IPF competition), plates [25,20,15,10,5,2.5,1.25], step 2.5. Dynamic programming over units of minPlate, with pair counts as bounds. Do not use greedy for lb (60 per side: greedy 45+10+5, best 35+25).; valid: target >= fixed. If the exact load isn't possible with the inventory, show the nearest loadable weight below and above.)
kept.correctedClaim: Plate loading: fixed = bar + 2 x collar; step = 2 x smallest plate; round the target to the nearest loadable weight, halve the remainder per side, and choose plates by a minimum-count search with inventory limits (heaviest innermost). lb defaults: bar 45, plates [45,35,25,10,5,2.5], step 5. kg defaults: bar 20, collars 0 in a gym (2.5 kg each in IPF competition), plates [25,20,15,10,5,2.5,1.25], step 2.5. Don't use heaviest-first for lb (60 per side: 45+10+5 vs 35+25). If the exact load is impossible, show the nearest loadable weights below and above.

sources.citation: IPF Technical Rulebook, effective 1 March 2026, section 2.3 Bars and Discs (bar + collars 25 kg; collars 2.5 kg each; discs 1.25-25 kg; heavier discs innermost).

kept.evidence: IPF Technical Rulebook 2026 (https://www.powerlifting.sport/fileadmin/ipf/data/rules/technical-rules/english/2026_IPF_Technical_Rulebook__effective_01_March_2026__v3.pdf): 2.3 'Weight of the bar and collars are to be 25 kg'; discs 1.25-25 kg; 'heavier discs innermost'; 2.4 Collars '(b) Must weigh 2.5 kg each' (section 2.4, not 2.3). Greedy failure verified by exhaustive script (see PL2). Equipment facts plus an algorithm, so C.

Round only for display, to the loadable step of the display unit. 45 lb = 20.41 kg; 20 kg = 44.09 lb (not the same bar).; valid: Exact by definition.)
kept.correctedClaim: Unit conversion: kg = lb x 0.45359237; lb = kg / 0.45359237 (exact by definition). Store the value in the unit it was entered in, together with the unit, and round only for display. 45 lb = 20.41 kg; 20 kg = 44.09 lb (different bars).

kept.evidence: NIST Handbook 44 (2026) Appendix B p. B-12 (https://www.nist.gov/system/files/documents/2025/12/30/appb-26-HB44-20251210.pdf): '1 avoirdupois pound = 0.453 592 37 kilogram.' Arithmetic checked: 20.4117 kg, 44.0925 lb. A definition, so C for consistency with PL3.

kept.formulaAsResearched: Fair PR detection: RM_best(e, r) = max over prior working sets s of exerciseId e with s.r >= r of s.w;  rep-max PR if w > RM_best(e, r).  Estimated PR if RTF <= 10 AND (rir known OR failure) AND e1RM_adj > max prior e1RM_adj(e) + minIncrement.  Weight PR if w > max prior w(e) with r >= 1. (defaults: Key by exerciseId, not name. Warm-ups excluded. Rep-max PRs (measured) rank above estimated PRs. minIncrement = 5 lb / 2.5 kg, so a rounding wobble can't count as a PR. Check r in 1..20 for rep-max PRs.; valid: Estimated PRs only for RTF <= 10. Rep-max PRs are valid at any rep count because they are observed, not modelled.)
kept.correctedClaim: Fair PR detection, keyed by exerciseId with warm-ups excluded. Rep-max PR: a set beats the heaviest prior weight done for at least that many reps (valid at any rep count because it is observed). Estimated PR: only when reps to failure <= 10, effort is known, and the new e1RM beats the old one by at least 5 lb / 2.5 kg. Rep-max PRs rank above estimated ones. The 10-rep limit follows Reynolds 2006; the rest are app definitions.

sources.citation: Reynolds JM et al. J Strength Cond Res 2006;20(3):584-592 (no more than 10 reps in 1RM prediction).

kept.evidence: Reynolds 2006, PMID 16937972 (Europe PMC): 'no more than 10 repetitions should be used in linear equations to estimate 1RM'. The PR definitions, the minIncrement buffer and the 1..20 rep check are conventions, so C.

kept.formulaAsResearched: Fatigue / deload signal (unvalidated convention): perf_i = best e1RM_adj of session i for lift L;  drop_i = perf_i / median(perf_{i-1}, perf_{i-2}, perf_{i-3}) - 1;  flag(L) if drop_i <= -0.05 AND drop_{i-1} <= -0.05;  suggest deload if flag on >= 2 lifts within 14 days OR user logs 'wiped out' on >= 2 sessions in 7 days (defaults: -5% threshold, 2 consecutive sessions, 2 lifts. None of these numbers were tested; they were chosen to sit above a 1-rep misjudgement (about 2.5-3.3% of e1RM). The suggested deload is 1 week of about half the sets at the same load (volume drops, load stays).; valid: Needs >= 4 logged sessions of the lift. Suggest only, never schedule automatically.)
kept.correctedClaim: Fatigue/deload signal (untested convention): per lift, compare the session's best RIR-adjusted e1RM with the median of the previous 3; flag if it is down 5% or more two sessions running; suggest a deload if 2+ lifts flag within 14 days or the user logs 'wiped out' in 2+ sessions within 7 days. None of these numbers were tested; the 5% sits above a one-rep misjudgement (about 2.5-3.3%). The suggested deload (1 week, about half the sets, same load) is one option coaches agree on, not a tested prescription. Needs 4+ logged sessions; suggest only, never schedule.

sources.citation: Bell L et al. Integrating deloading into strength and physique sports training programmes: an international Delphi consensus approach. Sports Med Open 2023;9:87.
Coleman M et al. Gaining more from doing less? The effects of a one-week deload period during supervised resistance training on muscular adaptations. PeerJ 2024;12:e16777.

kept.evidence: Bell 2023 (https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10511399/): coaches agreed deloads could be triggered by fatigue, volume could drop by lowering sets, and 'Training intensity could remain the same during the deload, but the volume may drop'; no numeric thresholds. Coleman 2024 (PMID 38274324) tested a full 1-week stop, not half sets, and found smaller lower-body strength gains. No source validates -5%, 2 sessions, 2 lifts or 'half the sets', so C.
